old_receipt.title: Compiling Expert Procedures into Verified Programs: When a Small Model Is Enough

new_receipt.title: Compiling Expert Procedures into Verified Programs: When a Small Model Is Enough

old.text: In procedural tool-use domains, how much of the gap between base models is procedure rather than capability? We build an explicit program from a teacher’s traces and run it in front of unchanged small models, including an 8B model. The construction, PLVR (Program Learning with Verifiable Rewards), takes the reasoning traces of a teacher, Kimi-K3, clusters their segments to locate recurring operations, has a frontier model author one typed primitive per operation, each run by a small frozen model and checked by a deterministic verifier, and assembles the program by A ∗ search over a rule library mined from the same traces, under a reference-action objective: the distance between the actions the program takes and the actions the teacher took on the training tasks. At inference the program takes one of two forms: for troubleshooting and tool search it produces the chain of thought the student would otherwise generate for itself, and the student acts on it; for multi-turn tool matching the student proposes each action and the program checks, repairs, or retries it before it goes out. On the official τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench Retail and Telecom test sets and on LiveMCPBench, with three Nemotron base models and the same program for each, the answer depends on the domain. On Telecom, Granite-4.2-8B as the student goes from 43.0% to 91.2% under the program, and every Nemotron student reaches 93.3–94.4%, against at most 58.2% for fine-tuning on the same traces, prompt optimisation of the student, or two token-matched baselines. With Granite-4.2-8B as the student, the program is within 2 to 3 points of the Nemotron students on Telecom and within 3 on Retail, and 3 to 13 points below them on LiveMCPBench: where the domain is procedural an 8B student is enough, and on tool search the student still matters. On Retail and LiveMCPBench the program is competitive with the best baseline. The spread between base models shrinks from about 7 points to about 2, averaged over the suites, with no weights changed.

old.text: Four results, all in Table 2 . First, on τ 2 \tau^{2} Telecom, Granite-4.2-8B as the student goes from 43.0% to 91.2% under the program, and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Nemotron 3 Nano, and Nemotron 3 Super reach 94.4%, 93.3%, and 93.3%; no other arm on any student exceeds 58.2%. Second, with Granite-4.2-8B as the student the program is 2.1 to 3.2 points below the Nemotron students on Telecom, within 2.7 points of them on Retail, and 3.2 to 12.6 points below on LiveMCPBench: where the domain is procedural an 8B student is enough, and on tool search the student still matters. On Retail and LiveMCPBench the program is competitive with the best baseline, above it on some students and below it on others. Third, the spread between the three students shrinks from 6.6 points to 1.9 averaged over the suites, with no weights changed; per suite, from 15.8 to 3.5 on Retail, 15.0 to 1.1 on Telecom, and 10.9 to 9.4 on LiveMCPBench. Fourth, the search contributes: on Lightning it takes the hand-written seed from 73.1%, 68.4%, and 37.9% on the three suites to 82.7%, 94.4%, and 50.5% (59.8% to 75.9% averaged).

old.text: Program-of-thought and PAL-style methods have a model emit executable code in place of free-text reasoning ( pal ; programofthoughts ) , and later work distils such programs into smaller models ( pad ) . These write the program to a fixed template per example. PLVR writes one program per task family, from operations mined out of the teacher’s traces, and runs it either to produce the reasoning the student then follows or, in its guard form, to check and repair the actions the student proposes; the second form is closer to runtime guardrails and output verifiers than to program-of-thought.

new.text: Program-of-thought and PAL-style methods have a model emit executable code in place of free-text reasoning ( Gao et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) , and later work distils such programs into smaller models ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) . These write the program to a fixed template per example. PLVR writes one program per task family, from operations mined out of the teacher’s traces, and runs it either to produce the reasoning the student then follows or, in its guard form, to check and repair the actions the student proposes; the second form is closer to runtime guardrails and output verifiers than to program-of-thought.

old.text: The three evaluation suites differ in the shape of their tasks, so we built a synthetic training set of 553 tasks in three subsets, one per kind of task (Table 1 ). The retail subset is 142 tasks in the τ 2 \tau^{2} retail format, multi-turn tool matching against a policy. The telecom subset is 178 tasks in the τ 2 \tau^{2} telecom format, mostly troubleshooting. The tool-search subset is 233 tasks in the LiveMCPBench format, tool search over a large registry. Each subset is split into training and held-aside tasks: 119/23 for retail, 122/56 for telecom, 183/50 for tool-search. No official τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench test task and no LiveMCPBench task appears in any subset.

new.text: The three evaluation suites differ in the shape of their tasks, so we built a synthetic training set of 553 tasks in three subsets, one per kind of task (Table 1 ). The retail subset is 142 tasks in the τ 2 \tau^{2} retail format, multi-turn tool matching against a policy. The telecom subset is 178 tasks in the τ 2 \tau^{2} telecom format, mostly troubleshooting. The tool-search subset is 233 tasks in the LiveMCPBench format, tool search over a large registry. Each subset is split into training and held-aside tasks: 119/23 for retail, 122/56 for telecom, 183/50 for tool-search.

Claude 5 Opus generated the tasks. For retail and telecom it used τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench’s own tools, environment, and policies and wrote new questions against them; for tool-search it used LiveMCPBench’s registry format and wrote new questions against that.
No benchmark task, and nothing that could stand in for one, appears in the training set:
No benchmark instances. Every benchmark task is excluded by id, including held-out ones. On LiveMCPBench the benchmark’s tasks were never read at all.
No shared underlying data. A training task may not reuse what a benchmark task is built on: the same issue type and fault set (telecom), or the same customer or order (retail).
No near-duplicates. Training task text is checked mechanically against benchmark text, and close matches are rewritten or dropped.
Held-aside tasks stay out. Each subset’s held-aside split is fixed up front and never used for training or search.
No uninformative tasks. Tasks that always pass or cannot be solved are removed.

old.text: Two arms spend the same tokens per task as the final program, with Granite-4.2-8B doing the extra work, so that the program is compared against other uses of the same budget on the same small model. ReAct runs a plan–act–reflect loop in the style of ReAct ( yao2023react ) : each turn, Granite-4.2-8B plans, the student acts from that plan placed where its own reasoning would go, and Granite critics review the action, with up to two revisions; the loop runs under the program’s Granite token budget (Appendix F ). Sample-and-judge samples five candidate responses and has Granite-4.2-8B, as a judge, select one, so that the total tokens match the program’s. The judge prompt is in Appendix G .

old.text: The three suites give different answers. On Telecom the program with Granite-4.2-8B as the student scores 91.2%, every Nemotron student under it 93.3–94.4%, and no other arm above 58.2%; the procedure is nearly the whole result, and an 8B model is enough to run it. Telecom is also where the program’s student runs longest, about 40 turns per task against about 9 on Retail. On Retail the program with Granite as the student scores 82.5%, within 2.7 points of the Nemotron students, so there too the choice of student matters little under the program, though the program’s margin over the baselines is small. On LiveMCPBench the program with Granite as the student reaches 42.1% and the Nemotron students are 3.2 to 12.6 points ahead of it; the student’s tool choice and argument binding still count. We read the part of the gap between base models that the program closes as an estimate of how much of that gap is procedure; the program also carries the frontier models’ prior knowledge (§ 5.6 ), so the estimate is an upper bound.

old.text: The gain is not attributed to the traces alone. The hand-written seed, Claude 5 Opus (which writes the primitives), and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (which mines the rules) all contribute, and neither frontier model is a blank slate about customer service or tool use; the ablation that removes the traces and the primitives still reaches 75.9% on Telecom (§ 5.6 ), and that ablation covers Retail and Telecom only. Inference under the program costs 5 to 10 times a vanilla run in FLOPs. All cells but the program’s Telecom cells are single runs, so differences of a few points are not resolved. The synthetic training tasks share the τ 2 \tau^{2} Retail and Telecom domains with the test suites and the LiveMCPBench format with LiveMCPBench, so domain knowledge can pass from the training set into the primitives, the rules, and the fine-tunes. The training tasks and their answers are different from the test tasks; the authors verified this.

We compiled a teacher’s procedure into a program rather than into a student’s weights: primitives authored by a frontier model from clusters of the teacher’s traces, each run by a small frozen model and verified as it runs, assembled by A ∗ over a rule library mined from the same traces under a reference-action objective, and used at inference to write the student’s chain of thought or to check the actions the student proposes. Run in front of three Nemotron base models and on its own, the one program estimates how much of each domain is procedure. On τ 2 \tau^{2} Telecom the estimate is that nearly all of it is: Granite-4.2-8B as the student goes from 43.0% to 91.2%, every Nemotron student reaches 93.3–94.4%, and no other arm passes 58.2%. On τ 2 \tau^{2} Retail the 8B student under the program is within 2.7 points of the Nemotron students; on LiveMCPBench the Nemotron students are 3 to 13 points ahead of it. On those two suites the program is competitive with the best baseline. No weights are updated, the program is the same for every base model, and the spread between base models shrinks where the program does the work. The program was produced once, at 3.0 × 10 19 3.0\times 10^{19} FLOPs, and costs 5 to 10 times a vanilla run to execute. Its output is a program rather than a checkpoint: it can be read at every step, it is the same for every base model, and it can be revised one primitive at a time.
